articles.title: Davi Alcolumbre rebate críticas do PL e cita urnas eletrônicas | G1
articles.standfirst: Presidente do Senado disse que urna só "serviu" quando o resultado foi a favor de apoiadores do senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ), derrotado na disputa da Presidência da República.
articles.summary: Davi Alcolumbre rebateu o senador Carlos Portinho, do PL, criticando o uso de agressões para fins eleitorais e a postura da oposição sobre as urnas eletrônicas.
articles.body:
O presidente do Senado Federal, Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP), disse nesta quarta-feira (4) que lamenta que políticos tenham se promovido durante as eleições ofendendo outras pessoas. Alcolumbre citou o resultado do primeiro turno do PL e fez sua fala depois de ter recebido críticas do líder do Partido Liberal (PL), Carlos Portinho (PL-RJ).

"Algumas vezes, alguns colegas nossos passam apenas do debate para as agressões em relação a esta presidência", disse ele. "Infelizmente, muitos atores políticos do meu país chamado Brasil se promoveram e ganharam a eleição ofendendo e agredindo as pessoas".

Segundo ele, as agressões buscam angariar apoio do "radicalismo horrível" que existe no Brasil. Alcolumbre disse ainda que estão prevalecendo as agressões, as ameaças e as mentiras.

"E para minha tristeza e de milhões de pessoas, ganharam as eleições, com base em alguma agenda específica, fosse ela contra o Judiciário, fosse ela contra o Executivo, fosse ela contra o presidente do Senado Federal, porque dava voto na eleição", disse Alcolumbre.

Em seguida, criticou falas que colocaram em dúvida o resultado das eleições, como fez o senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) depois do resultado do segundo turno:

"Abriu as urnas e ganharam a eleição, mas o pior de tudo isso é que no primeiro turno a urna eletrônica prestou [...] ela serviu para eleger 120 deputados federais do partido do candidato que perdeu a eleição, serviu para eleger 20 e tantos senadores, ela serviu para comemorar uma eleição vitoriosa do adversário do presidente Lula [...] e quando abriu no segundo turno, não prestou mais a urna", disse o presidente do Senado.

Alcolumbre discursou depois de o líder do PL cobrar a votação ainda nesta quarta-feira (4) de uma Proposta de Emenda à Constituição (PEC) para reduzir a maioridade penal. Mais cedo, Alcolumbre disse que não votaria o texto porque a Câmara começou a discussão antes do Senado.

Portinho criticou a decisão e disse que Alcolumbre estava descumprindo um acordo feito entre os líderes no dia anterior para acelerar a votação do tema. O PL defende a redução da maioridade penal para 14 anos em casos de crimes hediondos e para 16 para todos os outros crimes.

"O Senado hoje está submetido ao Poder Judiciário e à Câmara dos Deputados. E o presidente do Congresso, senhor Davi, o senhor é o presidente do Congresso, senador. Não é o presidente do Congresso, senhor Davi? O senhor é o presidente do Congresso, senador! Não é a Câmara dos Deputados que diz como vai ser, o Senado é a Casa Alta. O senhor fez um compromisso; compromisso é para ser cumprido", disse Portinho.

Para parte dos senadores, a fala foi um ataque à atuação de Alcolumbre. Parlamentares governistas o defenderam em discursos no plenário.

Depois, Portinho respondeu às falas de Alcolumbre e de seus colegas: “Eu não ofendi ninguém. Muito menos ofenderia à vossa Excelência [Alcolumbre], muito menos tratei aqui de urna eletrônica", disse o líder do PL.

Portinho defendeu ainda a fuga de Flávio para os Estados Unidos. Ele disse ainda que nenhum deles respondeu sobre o compromisso não foi cumprido.

articles.title: Com avanço democrata, Trump terá dificuldade em seguir com política externa atual, avaliam integrantes do governo Lula | G1
articles.standfirst: Interlocutores do Planalto preveem que oposição tente emparedar o presidente americano com a abertura de diversas frentes de investigação.
articles.summary: Interlocutores do Planalto preveem que oposição tente emparedar o presidente americano com a abertura de diversas frentes de investigação.
articles.body:
Após a vitória expressiva dos democratas nas eleições legislativas nos Estados Unidos , integrantes do governo brasileiro veem dificuldades no futuro de Donald Trump .

A expectativa é que o presidente americano tenha dificuldade em seguir com a política de imposição de tarifas e também com a implementação da chamada “Doutrina Donroe”, linha da política externa da Casa Branca que compreende o hemisfério ocidental, incluindo a América Latina, como zona de interesse norte-americano.

🔎 O Partido Democrata, de oposição ao governo republicano de Donald Trump, conquistou na madrugada desta quarta-feira (4) a maioria das cadeiras no Senado e na Câmara dos Deputados americanos. A vitória democrata incluiu a tomada de cadeiras historicamente ocupadas pelos republicanos e altera o equilíbrio de poder para a segunda metade do mandato de Trump à frente do país.

O Brasil não irá se manifestar oficialmente sobre o resultado das eleições de meio de mandato . Não é praxe da diplomacia brasileira publicar notas sobre eleições em outros países. Além disso, Brasil e Estados Unidos vivem uma crise diplomática há mais de um ano, e a linha do governo brasileiro é adotar o pragmatismo para não agravar as tensões.

Nos bastidores, no entanto, o resultado das eleições legislativas nos EUA foi recebido com entusiasmo por integrantes do governo Lula , que fazem um paralelo com a disputa presidencial brasileira.

“Foi um 7 a 1. Os piores cenários para Trump se confirmaram. Tanto lá como cá são sociedades que prezam suas democracias, e demonstraram no voto. Retificaram o rumo do delírio autoritário”, afirmou um diplomata brasileiro.

Comemoração de democratas após vitória nas eleições legislativas americanas — Foto: REUTERS

De forma reservada, a leitura de integrantes do governo que atuam no Itamaraty e na área internacional é que os democratas terão força para abrir no Congresso diversas frentes de investigação sobre ações de Trump nos dois primeiros anos de governo.

O entendimento é de que isso tende a forçar a Casa Branca a seguir com uma linha mais cautelosa nas políticas externa e tarifária daqui em diante.

Um integrante do governo que acompanha as negociações com o USTR (Escritório Comercial dos EUA) sobre as tarifas impostas ao Brasil afirmou que técnicos do escritório já vêm oferecendo resistência nos últimos meses a dar aval a tarifas “intempestivas e autoritárias” determinadas por Trump. Diante do risco maior de investigações, a burocracia estatal deverá resistir ainda mais a dar sustentação a essa agenda.

Interlocutores do governo lembram que muitos senadores e deputados democratas foram eleitos defendendo que haja investigação sobre as operações na América Latina, como, por exemplo, as ações na Venezuela que incluíram a captura de Nicolás Maduro e ataques a Caracas.

Após captura pelo governo americano, Nicolás Maduro responde a acusações de narcotráfico em Nova York, que ele nega e que podem levá-lo à prisão perpétua — Foto: Getty Images

Ações unilaterais que possam ferir a soberania dos países latino-americanos também tenderiam a perder espaço na segunda metade da administração Trump.

Outro tema que pode ser impactado é a regulamentação das 'big techs', grandes empresas multinacionais de tecnologia. O perfil dos eleitos indica que haverá uma coalizão em defesa da regulação dessas plataformas.

A medida tem apoio não só do Partido Democrata, mas também entre uma parcela dos parlamentares republicanos.

A pauta interessa ao governo Lula, que, nos últimos anos, tentou avançar com a regulamentação das plataformas, mas encontrou resistência no Congresso. A leitura no Palácio do Planalto é que a falta de regulação do setor favorece a direita mais ligada ao ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro (PL).

Auxiliares de Lula também preveem que Trump faça uma segunda metade do governo mais voltada para questões internas, e não para a política externa, uma vez que a Guerra do Irã é apontada como a grande causa da derrota republicana nas eleições legislativas americanas.

O presidente dos EUA, Donald Trump, discursa no canteiro de obras do salão de baile da Casa Branca. — Foto: Evan Vucci/Reuters

Sendo assim, a tendência, segundo estes interlocutores, é que Trump faça uma disputa política com os democratas em torno de temas relacionados a minorias – intensificando o discurso contra grupos como imigrantes, muçulmanos e a população LGBTQIA+ – e reduzindo a atenção sobre adversários externos, como Irã e Cuba.

O governo brasileiro vai observar, nos próximos dias, como a administração Trump vai absorver a derrota e reorientar sua atuação daqui para frente.

A partir disso, a diplomacia brasileira também irá calibrar suas estratégias na relação bilateral. Além do tarifaço, há diversos pontos de atrito entre os países, como a suspeita de que o governo americano tenha ajudado Flávio Bolsonaro a fugir do país e a suspensão do visto diplomático da embaixadora brasileira em Washington, Maria Luiza Viotti.

articles.title: Dino pede informações a Fachin para analisar pedidos para anular votos de Barroso e Rosa Weber em julgamento sobre aborto | G1
articles.standfirst: Entidades religiosas querem anular votos de Barroso e Rosa Weber para descriminalizar o aborto até 12 semanas de gestação e apontam falhas em procedimentos para sessão virtual.
articles.summary: Entidades religiosas querem anular votos de Barroso e Rosa Weber para descriminalizar o aborto até 12 semanas de gestação e apontam falhas em procedimentos para sessão virtual.
articles.body:
Ministro Flávio Dino, do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), em sessão plenária do 21 de outubro de 2026. — Foto: Gustavo Moreno/STF

O ministro Flávio Dino, do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), pediu nesta quarta-feira (4) que áreas técnicas da Corte prestem informações para que seja feita análise de pedidos de anulação de votos em um julgamento que discutiu a descriminalização do aborto voluntário nas primeiras 12 semanas de gestação.

Dino, que herdou a relatoria do caso, analisa questionamentos da União dos Juristas Católicos de São Paulo (UJUCASP), do Instituto Brasileiro de Direito e Religião (IBDR) e da Conferência Nacional dos Bispos do Brasil (CNBB) dos procedimentos adotados para análise, no plenário virtual, da ação em 17 de outubro de 2025, quando o então ministro Luís Roberto Barroso votou para liberar a interrupção da gestação nesse período .

O voto de Barroso foi dado um dia antes de sua aposentadoria.

Logo após a apresentação do voto de Barroso, o ministro Gilmar Mendes pediu que o tema fosse tratado no plenário presencial. Foi o segundo voto na Corte a favor da descriminalização do aborto voluntário nas primeiras 12 semanas de gestação.

Antes, essa posição foi defendida pela ministra Rosa Weber, primeira relatora da ação.

A União dos Juristas Católicos de São Paulo (UJUCASP) e o Instituto Brasileiro de Direito e Religião (IBDR) pedem para que o voto de Barroso seja considerado inválido. Argumentam que a abertura de sessão virtual às vésperas da aposentadoria do ministro, com a finalidade de viabilizar a apresentação de seu voto, comprometeu a imparcialidade do julgamento.

A CNBB também quer anular o voto de Rosa Weber. A justificativa é que o voto pela liberação do aborto só foi inserido no sistema do plenário virtual após um pedido para que o caso fosse julgado no plenário presencial. A CNBB afirma que não seria possível a apresentação de votos pelos demais integrantes da Corte após o destaque para o plenário presencial.

Segundo Dino, "verifico que as controvérsias processuais suscitadas pelos amici curiae [amigos da Corte] dizem respeito à regularidade dos atos que antecederam e determinaram a realização da sessão virtual extraordinária de 17 de outubro de 2025, inclusive quanto às providências adotadas no âmbito da presidência desta Corte".

Dino chamou a atenção para o fato de a sessão virtual ter sido incluída na pauta da ministra Rosa Weber, aposentada desde 2023. Segundo ele, a ministra "certamente não praticou qualquer ato em 2025" para incluir o processo na pauta de julgamento.

"Considerada em conjunto com as questões arguidas nas petições, evidencia a necessidade de esclarecimento da sequência de atos processuais e administrativos que culminaram na realização da sessão virtual extraordinária, bem como dos seus respectivos fundamentos constitucionais, legais e regimentais, a fim de assegurar a adequada apreciação das alegações de nulidade".

articles.title: CNJ: Certidão de óbito deve registrar morte em ação policial | G1
articles.standfirst: Além de causa médica, documento deve registrar intervenções de órgãos de segurança. Medida deve impactar registros sobre letalidade policial e também reparação.
articles.summary: A decisão do CNJ sobre a certidão de óbito em ação policial busca dar transparência à letalidade estatal e facilitar o acesso de famílias a reparações e benefícios.
articles.body:
O Conselho Nacional de Justiça (CNJ) determinou que as certidões de óbito de pessoas mortas em ações policiais terão que registrar expressamente que a ocorrência foi motivada ou que a morte foi fruto de intervenção de órgãos de segurança pública.

Atualmente, os registros de mortes nessas circunstâncias anotam apenas a causa médica, sem o contexto do óbito. Agora, com a determinação do conselho, as duas questões terão que constar no documento.

🚨 A regra se aplica, por exemplo, para vítimas de disparos de arma de fogo em ações policiais e casos de desaparecimento nessas circunstâncias em que a morte presumida seja validada pelo Poder Judiciário.

A resolução, aprovada por unanimidade no plenário virtual do conselho, estabelece que a morte em decorrência ou no contexto de intervenção dos órgãos de segurança pública é aquela causada direta, ou indiretamente por agentes das:

A medida também vale para outras categorias ou instituições que tenham poder de polícia relacionada à segurança.

O CNJ também proibiu que esses registros nas certidões utilizem expressões estigmatizantes, criminalizantes ou que naturalize a violência, como “auto de resistência”, “resistência seguida de morte”, “confronto”, “oposição” à intervenção policial.

A orientação do conselho é que seja adotada a seguinte redação: “morte não natural, violenta, ocorrida em decorrência ou no contexto de intervenção de órgão de segurança pública, nos termos do título apresentado”.

Policiais do Bope atuam em operação na Penha - 28/10/2025 — Foto: Aline Massuca/Reuters

A decisão também permite a retificação de certidões de pessoas mortas nessa condição quando houver decisão judicial que reconheça a causa da ação policial

A ideia é garantir maior transparência, monitoramento e controle dos registros públicos sobre a letalidade estatal, além de garantir acesso a reparações e benefícios.

A inclusão do dado no registro não implica reconhecimento automático de responsabilidade civil, administrativa ou penal do Estado, ou de agentes públicos.

Relator da proposta, o presidente do CNJ e do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), ministro Edson Fachin, afirmou que a medida é um avanço concreto no enfrentamento à violência de Estado e ao fortalecimento da proteção às vítimas e aos familiares pelo sistema de justiça.

"O fenômeno atinge sobretudo a população jovem, negra e periférica. A omissão compromete a fidedignidade do registro público e impõe às famílias o ônus de provar repetidamente as circunstâncias do óbito para acessar reparações e benefícios. Também priva o Estado de dados confiáveis para políticas de prevenção", escreveu.

Fachin disse que a medida cumpre obrigações da Convenção Americana sobre Direitos Humanos, deve auxiliar o desenvolvimento de políticas públicas voltadas à redução das mortes decorrentes de ações de segurança pública e não antecipa juízo sobre eventual responsabilidade civil, administrativa ou penal, que terão que ser apurados em procedimentos próprios na Justiça.

articles.title: McGuire flips California House seat in redistricting shake-up
articles.summary: Democrat Mike McGuire is projected to win California’s 1st District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). McGuire defeated Republican Rep. James Gallagher,...
articles.body:
Democrat Mike McGuire is projected to win California's 1st District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

McGuire defeated Republican Rep. James Gallagher, flipping a Northern California seat that became a prime Democratic pickup opportunity following a contentious redistricting battle . For Gallagher, the defeat marks an abrupt end to a short stint in Washington.

DDHQ reported McGuire leading Gallagher by over 16 points with 49 percent of ballots counted.

The Republican won a special election in June to replace Rep. Doug LaMalfa (R-Calif.), who died in January after representing the region for more than a decade.

But the district Gallagher won over the summer looked dramatically different from the one voters weighed in on this week.

California voters approved Proposition 50 late last year, temporarily redrawing the state's congressional map in response to a Republican-led redistricting push that began in Texas at President Trump's urging.

The new boundaries brought more Democratic voters into the 1st District, including portions of Sonoma and Mendocino counties, while shifting several Republican strongholds into neighboring districts.

Under the previous boundaries, Trump carried the district by roughly 25 percentage points in 2024. The new map would have favored former Vice President Kamala Harris by approximately 12 points.

DDHQ rated the race as "safe Democratic" ahead of Election Day.

McGuire, a California state Senate leader, has served in the state Legislature since 2014 and previously held local offices in Sonoma County, including mayor of Healdsburg, Calif. His campaign focused heavily on opposition to Trump's agenda, including federal healthcare cuts and tariffs, while also emphasizing wildfire prevention and affordability.

Gallagher, meanwhile, criticized the redistricting effort and sought to highlight his record representing rural Northern California communities.

articles.title: Democrats flipped US Senate. Will John Fetterman upset their control?
articles.summary: Democrats won control of the U.S. Senate on Nov. 3. If U.S. Sen. John Fetterman leaves the party, here's what could happen to that control.
articles.body:
With Democrats winning control of the U.S. Senate , flipping seats blue in traditionally red states like Texas, Kansas and South Carolina, where does that leave U.S. Sen. John Fetterman after Election Day 2026?

Fetterman, a Democrat from Pennsylvania elected in 2022, regularly breaks with his party — often enough that it's caused widespread speculation about whether or not he'll become a Republican or an independent.

In recent months, he's been the deciding voice on multiple occasions in the Senate, repeatedly blocking war powers resolutions meant to stop President Donald Trump from attacking Iran without congressional oversight.

Now that Democrats have control of the Senate, with a total of 54 seats compared to the Republicans' 44 seats, with races in Alaska and Mississippi yet to be called, here's how Fetterman's influence could change.

With Democrats flipping the Senate, how much power does Fetterman's vote have?

Because Fetterman often breaks from Democrats to vote with Republicans, there was speculation ahead of the election that even if Democrats flipped the Senate, the party may still struggle to get measures passed because of him.

See Sen. John Fetterman's career in Pennsylvania, US Congress

U.S. Senator John Fetterman (D-PA) speaks to reporters on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., on the day of classified briefings for the full U.S. Senate and House of Representatives on the situation in Iran.

But because Democrats won seats across the country and now have a strong majority in the Senate, Fetterman's vote alone won't be enough to be the deciding factor on Democrat-led measures.

What happens if Fetterman changes parties?

Fetterman could change parties if he wanted and join more than 20 other senators who have done the same, including Kyrsten Sinema , I-Arizona, and Joe Manchin , I-West Virginia, two former senators who left the Democratic Party to become independents in the early 2020s during their time in office.

Ultimately, the Democrats will still control the Senate regardless of whether or not Fetterman leaves the party.

As of Nov. 4, Fetterman has not said that he will change parties — in fact, he's denied that he will do so, though that hasn't stopped speculation about his loyalty to Democrats, as well as encouragement from Trump for him to become a Republican.

"It's gonna be hard for him to get the nomination as a Democrat, but I'd love to have him as a Republican," Trump said to reporters at Joint Base Adrews on Oct. 10. "If you look at the polls, he does better as a Republican than he does as a Democrat."

In September, Fetterman shouted at reporters over the topic. In a video published by CSPAN on X, Fetterman raised his voice, telling reporters, "I'm not going to be a Republican. You know, why can't you guys just wait 'til the midterm? And if I turn a Republican, then I'll be a liar, then."

Time and time again, Fetterman has repeatedly broken from the Democratic Party to vote with Republicans.

Fetterman has voted numerous times since the start of the year to stop Congress from limiting Trump's ability to attack Iran without oversight, sometimes casting the deciding vote. He's cleared the way for Trump nominees to take high-level positions, voting to confirm Pam Bondi as U.S. attorney general, Kristi Noem as secretary of the Department of Homeland Security, Markwayne Mullin as Noem's replacement and more.

A staunch supporter of Israel, Fetterman has said that if Democrats stop showing support for Israel, he will leave the party.

"If they put that in our platform — no aid for Israel — and officially become the anti-Israel party, then yeah, that's a red line for me," Fetterman told NBC News . "Democrats, we always should support Israel. That's our special ally, you know? In the only democracy in the entire region, that's Israel. So I'm always proud to stand with Israel."

articles.title: Ukrainian strikes kill three in Russia’s Belgorod region
articles.summary: Russian strikes also cut power to Ukrainian cities as Moscow claims 700 Ukrainian drones downed across multiple regions.
articles.body:
Ukrainian drone strikes have killed three people in Russia’s Belgorod region, while attacks cut power to multiple cities in Ukraine and parts of Russian-occupied Crimea, officials reported.

Local Russian authorities in Belgorod, which borders Ukraine, announced the three deaths on Wednesday. In Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia’s overnight attacks damaged power generation facilities and substations in nine regions leaving emergency outages in many cities.

Russia’s Defence Ministry confirmed on Telegram that it hit two power stations in Ukraine’s Kyiv and Zhytomyr regions. Ukraine has repeatedly said Moscow is targeting its energy grid as temperatures drop before winter.

Overnight, Russian attacks on critical infrastructure caused hours-long power and water outages across Kyiv and surrounding regions.

Residents in the capital were urged to use public drinking water fountains, and emergency centres offering hot tea and power points to charge devices were set up in the worst-hit areas.

There were also power outages in Crimea, the peninsula Russia seized from Ukraine in 2014, home to approximately 2.5 million residents. Russia’s Ministry of Energy said Ukrainian strikes hit energy infrastructure overnight and that temporary outage schedules were in force. It did not say how many households were affected.

But reports also indicated that Russia-held Crimea ordered power cuts after an accident outside the region, a Moscow-installed ⁠official said, according to the Reuters news agency.

‌In addition to the capital, Kyiv, Russia also hit the regions of Poltava, Dnipro, Kirovohrad and Rivne, Reuters reported, citing Ukraine’s emergency service and local officials.

In southern Russia, a Ukrainian drone attack started a fire at a major warehouse belonging to Ozon, known as Russia’s Amazon. The strikes were on an Ozon distribution facility in the town of Adygeysk, in the Republic of Adygea, regional head Murat Kumpilov said.

Ozon said all workers were evacuated and no one was hurt, and that it had removed damaged goods from its listings and rerouted deliveries.

Russia’s Defence Ministry also said it downed 709 Ukrainian drones across 14 regions, Crimea and the Black and Azov seas.

Amid ongoing fighting between Russia and Ukraine, Russia’s Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the Kremlin hopes United States President Donald Trump will continue his peace efforts after a sweeping Democratic victory in the congressional midterms dealt a blow to the president.

“President Trump continues to exercise his powers. We sincerely hope that he will also continue his peacemaking efforts,” Peskov said in a statement.

Whether a change in Congress could hinder Trump’s peace efforts, Peskov said, as cited by the state-run Interfax news outlet, that it was “an internal matter for America”.

Democratic control of the legislature in January is expected to bring a more vocal pro-Kyiv majority in Congress that could pressure Trump to change tack, but there is little hope that the US will return as a major financial backer of Ukraine.

Meanwhile, Ukraine’s Zelenskyy awarded US First Lady Melania Trump the Order of Princess Olga, which honours women who have contributed to Ukraine, according to a presidential decree on Wednesday.

The decree noted Melania Trump’s “significant personal contribution” in providing support for humanitarian aid and children in Ukraine.

Ukrainian officials say the US first lady played a pivotal role in organising a six-day local ceasefire to evacuate civilians from the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky, which ended on Sunday.

articles.title: Johnson: GOP will take back House in 2028, ‘finish the job’
articles.summary: House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said Wednesday he thinks Republicans will take back the House in two years despite a Democratic blowout in this year’s midterms. “This Democrat House majority will be led by the most radical and extreme leftists in American history. However, Republicans will never stop fighting to defend the Constitution and protect…
articles.body:
House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said Wednesday he thinks Republicans will take back the House in two years despite a Democratic blowout in this year’s midterms.

“This Democrat House majority will be led by the most radical and extreme leftists in American history. However, Republicans will never stop fighting to defend the Constitution and protect the foundations that have made America the greatest nation in the history of the world,” the Speaker said in an early-morning post to the social platform X.

“We will continue pressing forward with our agenda of common sense, and our vision to make America great again—and come 2028, we WILL take back the House and we will finish the job,” he added.

The congressional map was painted blue Tuesday, with the Democrats reclaiming both the House and Senate — and securing a chance to restrict President Trump’s power in the latter half of his second term.

The Democrats’ wins came amid challenging political territory for the GOP, with Republicans dragged down by issues such as the unpopular war in Iran, Trump’s slumping approval numbers and concerns about the cost of living.

Democrats are projected to finish with 258 seats in the House and 55 seats in the Senate , according to Decision Desk HQ.

articles.title: Vance breaks silence on midterms: ‘The reason we lost is the war’
articles.summary: Vice President Vance on Wednesday blamed the ongoing Iran war for the Republican Party’s abysmal results in the midterm elections, brushing off other issues that appeared to tank GOP candidates, including the Trump administration’s harsh immigration policies. “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance said in a…
articles.body:
Vice President Vance on Wednesday blamed the ongoing Iran war for the Republican Party’s abysmal results in the midterm elections, brushing off other issues that appeared to tank GOP candidates, including the Trump administration’s harsh immigration policies.

“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance said in a lengthy social media post.

“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest,” he continued.

“But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”

The president’s son, Donald Trump Jr., shortly thereafter agreed with Vance’s assessment, writing on X above the original post: “Every word of this is [100, 100, 100 percent].”

President Trump earlier had partially blamed the Iran war for the GOP’s sweeping midterm losses , even as he stood defiant and said he would have done it again.

Trump told The Wall Street Journal that the Middle East conflict, now in its eighth month, “was a piece of it” in an election night interview .

Asked later Tuesday about Vance’s post and whether he knew it was coming, Trump said: “I know how he feels about [the Iran war]. I think it was fine. I thought it was good.”

Speaking to reporters in the White House ballroom, which is in the midst of construction, Trump said he knew the war would impact voting but “whether it impacted it or not Iran can’t have a nuclear weapon, and they will never have a nuclear weapon.”

He added that the war will end “whenever I want it to, but it’s gotta be done right.”

Administration officials have quickly sought to deflect blame for Republicans’ trouncing, the likes of which has not been seen by either party in a midterm election in the last 50 years. The results are widely seen as a referendum on Trump’s presidency.

The war has sent gas and diesel prices soaring in the U.S. and globally since it began in late February, increasing voter frustrations after the president campaigned on ending foreign wars and lowering prices in 2024.

A longtime skeptic of U.S. intervention abroad, Vance has sought to publicly distance himself from the deeply unpopular conflict ahead of a possible 2028 presidential run. Early in the war , it was reported that he was dubious of and opposed to the U.S. striking Tehran as Trump mulled whether to do so.

After the war began, Vance publicly defended Operation Epic Fury, though in recent months he has attempted to steer clear of the topic.

In his post to X on Tuesday, he insisted that despite the major GOP losses, “data analysts on our side” showed in the lead up to voting that “in some states turnout was merely OK, in other states it was downright amazing, and in no state was it catastrophic,” adding that “there was a genuine sense of optimism on our team.”

But he said the main problem wasn’t turnout but that “many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026” due to anger over the Iran war, cost of living and inflation, not focusing on putting America first and the current U.S. relationship with Israel.

In pointing their fingers back at Trump, Republican lawmakers have said the war, the administration’s tariff policies, overfocusing on pet projects such as the White House ballroom and supporting weak candidates for the midterms ruined the GOP’s chances of keeping control of Congress.

The result was Republicans losing at least seven Senate seats, Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) projected. Two Senate races, Mississippi and Alaska, remain uncalled as of Wednesday morning.

The GOP also lost 30 seats in the House, with more than 20 races left to be projected, according to DDHQ.

“There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why that is. One of the pollsters I really respect told me that our economic messaging wasn’t sharp enough down the stretch. I’m sure that’s true,” Vance admitted.

He predicted “a lot of gaslighting” in the next few months from establishment politicians saying “the solution to our woes is amnesty.”

“I’m open to the idea that we should change enforcement — by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance. But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you,” he claimed.

Despite the gargantuan losses, Vance said he remained hopeful for the U.S.

“To the people who are pissed off and want to say, ‘I told you so’: you’re right, you did tell us so. Take that energy into electing Republicans who share your worldview. To the people who are just pissed at the results, you should be. Let’s take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country,” he wrote.

articles.title: House Majority Leader Steve Scalise will run for minority leader
articles.summary: House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) will run for minority leader, setting up what will likely be a contentious contest against House Judiciary Committee Chair Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) for the position. A source familiar with Scalise’s plans shared them with The Hill, swiftly following news that Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) told staff on Wednesday morning…
articles.body:
House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) will run for minority leader, setting up what will likely be a contentious contest against House Judiciary Committee Chair Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) for the position.

A source familiar with Scalise’s plans shared them with The Hill, swiftly following news that Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) told staff on Wednesday morning he would not run for the post .

Scalise served as House minority whip from 2019 to 2022, when Democrats controlled the House, before ascending as majority leader in 2023 after Republicans won the lower chamber back. He has been one of Johnson’s closest allies, serving as his right-hand man in navigating the divisions within the House GOP conference and advancing President Trump’s legislative agenda.

Scalise initially won the Republican nomination to be Speaker in 2023, beating Jordan in a secret ballot vote. But he withdrew from the race when it became clear he would not win enough support from his conference to get the votes needed on the House floor.

He wrote in a letter to his Republican colleagues on Wednesday that “last night’s election was far worse than any of us expected.”

“We fought hard and left it all on the field, but clearly, we were unable to defy history,” Scalise said. “Despite all we accomplished together, we will now find ourselves in the minority along with losing some incredible friends and public servants…it is more important now than ever for us to emerge from this stronger and united because the stakes couldn’t be higher,” he said.

Scalise warned that “socialists are coming to Washington with a radical agenda that threatens the America we hold dear,” and that he’s running for minority leader to lead Republicans back to the majority.

“They will stop at nothing to undo the progress we’ve made alongside President Trump over the last two years,” Scalise wrote. “The House Republican Conference must be the first line of defense in this crucial battle, and we must fight like our way of life depends on it – because it does.”

articles.title: Democrats seize majority of governors’ offices in election-night shift
articles.summary: Democrats flipped enough governorships to seize a majority, reversing a 26-24 Republican edge and shifting state government power opposite the White House.
articles.body: Democrats will hold a majority of the nation’s governorships after a series of victories on election night, shifting control of one of the most influential levels of government in the country to the political party opposite of the White House. As of Wednesday morning, Democrats controlled 28 governorships to Republicans' 20. Two races, Kansas and Alaska, have yet to be called. The results mark a significant reversal from the political landscape heading into the election, when Republicans held 26 governors’ offices compared with 24 for Democrats. Democrats needed a net gain of at least two seats to take the majority. While congressional control typically generates the most attention, governors across the country play a central role in setting state policy, approving or vetoing legislation, managing state agencies and directing responses to major issues, including public safety, education, healthcare, immigration and abortion. They also oversee state elections and frequently serve as the most prominent political figures in their states. The Democratic gains will give the party greater influence over policy in state capitals across the country, even as Republicans continue to control many state legislatures. The impact of the shift will vary by state, particularly in places where the governor’s party does not control both chambers of the legislature. The election-night results in gubernatorial races across the country could also play a role in the 2028 election cycle as Democrats will have a broader bench of governors to potentially choose from ahead of the 2028 presidential contest. Governors often become national party leaders, presidential contenders, and prominent surrogates during congressional and White House campaigns. A BLUE WAVE IN GOVERNORS' MANSIONS COULD HURT FAMILIES MORE THAN A BLUE CONGRESS The new balance could also intensify battles between Democratic governors and the Republican-led federal government on issues such as immigration enforcement, environmental regulations, education policy and federal funding. Republicans, meanwhile, will be forced to defend a smaller share of the nation’s governorships in the next election cycle while working to prevent further losses in states where Democrats made gains. 100 DAY SPRINT TO THE MIDTERMS KICKS OFF AS REPUBLICANS AND DEMOCRATS CLASH FOR CONTROL ACROSS THE COUNTRY The shift does not automatically translate into unified Democratic control of state governments. In many states, legislative majorities, attorneys general and other elected officials will continue to shape how much power governors can exercise. But the outcome represents a clear expansion of Democratic influence in state government and provides the party with a broader platform to advance its agenda nationwide. articles.title: ARI FLEISCHER: A Democratic majority means a mad dash to the left for 2028
articles.summary: Medicare for all, ICE abolition and Supreme Court expansion are set to become Democratic priorities as the 2028 presidential primary heats up.
articles.body: Now that the Democrats have taken control of Congress, expect limited action on the legislative front. While Trump’s agenda and his appointments are certainly stymied, the President still has a veto, so nothing happens unless the President wants it to happen. But that’s not the story you should keep an eye on. Instead, look out for the influence Congressional Democrats will have on the Democratic presidential primary, which begins now. Recall the last time there was a contested Democratic presidential primary, in 2019 and 2020, a record 29 Democratic candidates declared presidential runs. LIZ PEEK: THERE MAY BE A SILVER LINING TO TRUMP'S BRUTAL MIDTERM DEFEAT The earliest was on August 10, 2017, when former Congressman John Delaney (D-MD) jumped the gun and became the first declared candidate, way before the 2018 midterm was held. He was followed by Andrew Yang, who also announced the year prior to the mid-term. They were followed by Elizabeth Warren’s announcement of her exploratory committee in December 2018. Before January 2019 was over, six more candidates jumped in, including Kamala Harris. Bernie Sanders announced in February 2019 and eventual winner, Joe Biden, entered in late April. Get ready for a repeat this cycle. The 2027-2028 race will kick off now, and it’s likely there will be more than 20 Democratic candidates in the running. Just as Donald Trump in 2015 broke the Republican Party and ushered in a populist era, the Democratic Party, even after this 2026 win, is about to break. The old Democratic Party is receding, as the newly ascendant, redistributive socialists and progressives push to get their way. Look for Democrats to push the envelope everywhere. Compromising with Trump is not in the Democrats’ DNA, especially not after the rout the GOP just suffered. The Democrats’ significant majorities won’t shield them from the energy the left has on the party. Democrats run as moderates, but then govern from the left. See Jon Ossoff in Georgia. James Talarico and Abdul el Sayed are not going to vote purple. They’re as blue as you get. It won’t matter next year if their legislation doesn’t have enough votes to overcome a veto. Passing laws isn’t the goal. Preparing for 2028 is. The Democrats in 2027 will step into the on-deck circle of governance and politics. If they go too far, they’ll get hit by their own pitch. REPORTER’S NOTEBOOK: A DEMOCRATIC MAJORITY COULD EXPOSE THE LIMITS OF THE PROGRESSIVE AGENDA Medicare for All, the abolition of ICE and cutting off support for Israel are catnip for the Democrats. They will be Democratic priorities, even if the votes aren’t there. Democratic presidential contenders will call on Congress to pass these measures, and Congressional leaders will be pressured by rank and file to take them up. The filibuster will likely be eliminated, allowing for passage of an expansion of the Supreme Court, statehood for Democratic strongholds, and nationwide billionaire and millionaire taxes. They’ll get vetoed, but in failing, the Democrats will seek to set themselves up for future legislative success. When President Reagan in 1980 ran on supply-side tax cuts, he supported what, at that time, had been unsuccessful legislative initiatives launched by former Congressman Jack Kemp (R-NY) and Senator William Roth (R-DE) to cut taxes in the late 1970s. President Obama’s push for Obamacare was made possible by years of Democrats in the House and Senate who unsuccessfully pushed for expansion of health insurance in the individual marketplace, while prohibiting insurance companies from denying coverage based on a patient’s prior medical condition. President Trump’s success in shutting down illegal immigration was made possible by years of Republicans calling for President Obama to secure the border. Obama didn’t do it, but Republicans were ready, and they supported President Trump when he did. Congress’ mad dash to the left will create a mutual admiration society between the most ardent left-wingers in the House and Senate and the party’s presidential candidates. Candidates will call on the Congress to pass left wing measures so they can define themselves to primary voters, and Members of the House will endorse candidates who support their cause. They’ll be stampeded as the new Congress takes shape, with Socialists on the ascendancy and progressives in charge. President Trump ended the reign of establishment Republicans in 2016. An equivalent shift will take place among Democrats in 2027 and 2028. But their leftward lurching ship has been launched. Good luck stopping it now.

articles.title: US midterm results a 'victory' for Canadians hopeful of tariff relief
articles.summary: With Canada-US trade talks back on, Tuesday’s midterm Democratic wave puts pressure on the White House to come to a deal.
articles.body:
It was the midterm result that many in Canada had hoped for - a Democratic sweep that was in part a repudiation by American voters of Donald Trump's tariff on close trade allies.

"I was doing cartwheels down the street," said Ontario Premier Doug Ford on Wednesday morning, calling it "a victory for Canada".

Tuesday night's result is unlikely to grant Canada relief from those tariffs any time soon, but there is anticipation that the political shifts could create a more favourable environment for Ottawa to get the best deal now that on-again-off-again trade talks are back on.

US voters cited affordability as a main concern heading into the midterms and a survey by the Cato Institute in September suggested that about 75% believe the tariffs have raised prices.

In states like Maine and Michigan, tariffs played a significant role in the hard-fought races.

In Maine, incumbent Republican Senator Susan Collins clashed with the White House over tariffs.

She successfully lobbied to have some duties that directly affected the state removed, including on road salt, refrigeration equipment and seaweed, but in the end lost to Democrat Troy Jackson.

A similar story played out in Michigan, where state's the automobile manufacturing industry is deeply intertwined with Canada's - and where Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers.

In Ohio, Senator-elect Sherrod Brown, who defeated Republican Jon Husted, called the levies a "disaster" and vowed to slash costs for voters by getting rid of them .

Democratic leaders like Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer, now newly empowered, have both pushed to rein in the tariffs on Canada in recent months.

Still, Democratic control of Congress might not do much to move the needle on tariffs. Trump's levies have been largely enacted using executive orders without approval from Congress.

And speaking to Fox News on Tuesday night, Trump touted his "ultimate power" of veto to shut down bills passed by Congress that he does not like.

Some Democratic lawmakers have also supported certain tariffs in the past as a way to protect American manufacturing jobs, and could back keeping some in place.

There are currently several layers of tariffs on Canada, notably on sectors like autos, steel, aluminium and forestry.

After trade talks between Ottawa and Washington collapsed in August, the Trump administration imposed an additional 50% tariff on $20bn (£15bn) worth of various Canadian goods, from dairy to cosmetics and furniture.

The US also declared a total import ban on motorcycles, whey protein and alcohol.

Canada retaliated by slapping the US with its own 50% "dollar-for-dollar" tariffs. Most provinces have also banned the sale of US alcohol in retaliation.

Trump had also previously threatened to escalate the trade war with Canada further by ⁠raising tariffs on sectors, including auto manufacturing, as of 1 January.

There were signs that his administration had become more sensitive to the optics of its tariffs on Canada in the run up to the election.

Just a few days before the vote, Trump told reporters that a trade deal is "very close" after speaking with Prime Minister Mark Carney.

Speaking to reporters on Tuesday evening, Carney said of US negotiators that "they're asking less and they're offering more" in recent discussions.

On Wednesday, US-Canada Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said the midterm results won't change anything in the short term, and dismissed speculation over what the new Congress might do when they're seated in the new year as "an interesting discussion at a faculty club luncheon".

"Our approach will not change and we don't intend to speculate on the approach being taken by the Americans," he said.

Pierre Poilievre, leader of Canada's Conservatives, said on Wednesday that "nobody controls Donald Trump".

But he said that midterms results show Canada has "massive leverage" given that the tariffs are broadly unpopular.

"We've got to use that goodwill to pressure for tariff-free trade," he said.

Trump may indeed feel more pressure to sign a deal with Canada now that American voters have clearly communicated their frustration, said Colin Robertson, a former Canadian diplomat and a fellow at the Canadian Global Affairs Institute.

"Will this change Trump's mind? It might, because he suffered such a beating at the polls."

But he added it remains to be seen how Trump will react from the bruising midterm loss.

Canada has an ideal window between now and January - when the new Democratic lawmakers are sworn in - to finalise a deal, Robertson noted.

After that, Trump is likely to be distracted by investigations launched by Democrats into Trump's family and finances and some members of his administration, Robertson said.

US trade representative Jamieson Greer also said earlier this year that he had ambitions to have interim deals in place with Canada and Mexico around the North American free trade deal, known as the USMCA in the US and CUSMA in Canada, before the end of the year.

And while Carney struck a more optimistic tone in recent days on the current state of Canada-US trade talks, he also told Politico last month that he was prepared to wait for a new American president if necessary to reach a deal with the US.

articles.title: The new Congress may struggle to push a progressive agenda
articles.summary: Major change on key issues, such as Israel-Palestine, will be limited by the president and the Democratic establishment.
articles.body:
As the dust settles on the 2026 US midterm elections, two facts are clear: First, the Democrats have achieved a historic victory – and second, Donald Trump remains president for the coming two years.

That means Congressional Democrats will have three legislative lanes to pursue: The first is constraining Trump. This includes doing what they can through Congress to bring the Iran war to a conclusion, blocking many of his nominations, particularly to the judiciary, ending ICE’s aggressive immigrant detentions, and pursuing oversight of Trump and his allies’ financial networks and alleged corruption.

The second lane will be about demonstrating a positive policy agenda to inform the 2028 cycle, when Trump will be off the ballot. This is more about “messaging bills” focused on social issues, but could also include economic measures such as tax reform proposals, as well as significant reforms of US global defence cooperation authorities and shifts to major foreign policy questions, such as aid to Israel.

The final lane will be that – perhaps narrow – set of issues where bipartisanship and cooperation with the White House is possible. Putting guardrails around America’s burgeoning artificial intelligence (AI) sector may fit in that box, although some of Trump’s biggest funders are likely to do what they can to derail progress.

Many of the bills that will be put forward in the first and second lanes would be subject to presidential veto. Others will be toned down, as the Democratic establishment seeks to resist the progressive left’s ambitious agenda. These dynamics are likely to make the upcoming Congress less productive.

On foreign policy, in particular, Congress is able to pass just a slim set of acts without presidential endorsement, such as war powers legislation, limiting the president’s ability to wage war without Congressional approval; or measures like the recent Senate resolution advanced by Maryland Democrat Chris Van Hollen to demand reporting on Israel’s human rights record; or committee subpoenas, which can be used to investigate members of the Trump administration for wrongdoing. But they are likely to be ignored or stonewalled by the White House, leading to months, if not years, of fruitless litigation.

That is not to say that introducing “stand-alone” bills on issues, such as arms transfers to Israel, would not be important even if blocked by the president. They remain useful both for framing the conversation and for getting members of Congress on the record and establishing consensus positions.

In the Senate, where several incumbents are likely to throw their hats into the upcoming presidential nomination contest, such bills could be used to highlight the progressive credentials of some candidates – or to force more conservative members into awkward positions. That might ultimately make a difference in terms of the framing and debate for the 2028 election – and a potential Democratic administration thereafter. But it will not change anything in the immediate term.

There are at least three tools available to legislators where a fierce – and perhaps impactful – debate is likely to play out. The first is that enabled by Congress’ constitutional “power of the purse”. If the current Republican majorities do not manage to pass an annual funding bill by the end of this calendar year, the Democrats will have both the current year and the next two years of US government funding under their control.

This includes, of course, Israel’s annual allocation of $3.3bn, which Trump himself put into doubt in a surprising and as yet unclarified statement on election day. If nothing else, the president’s call for an end to security assistance to Israel may accelerate what would likely have been a steady reduction under Democratic leadership.

The new Congress will also be able to reconsider a range of funding restrictions and requirements, such as the prohibition on funding the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees (UNRWA), or the limitations on funding the Palestinian Authority.

Passing such bills will not be simply a matter of partisan rancour — we can expect some pretty tough battles to play out within the Democratic caucus itself on some of these issues. Then it is another matter of whether the Trump administration adheres to the law with the funding it ultimately receives.

The second area to watch is that of oversight. With the majority in hand, Democrats in the House and Senate can set the agenda – deciding which actions by the Trump administration are ripe for investigation, identifying witnesses, and using the committee gavels to drive the public debate.

Party leadership will be eager to focus on the issues that are most damaging to the current administration and its likely candidates for succession, such as Vice President JD Vance or Secretary of State Marco Rubio, while being least disruptive to party unity.

And because the system relies on seniority, control of the agenda of Congressional committees that can investigate the government would rest with Democratic establishment members who would be less likely than their newer or younger peers to be critical of the US-Israel relationship.

That said, it is hard to imagine a Democratic Congress that does not at least conduct oversight of Trump’s Board of Peace and its opaque sources of funding and influence. Another likely topic is the question of US involvement in the current war with Iran.

What the Democrats choose not to pursue via oversight will also be important: The weaponisation of anti-Semitism by the current and previous Congress to attack the US education sector and civil society should come to an end under the next Congress. Though certainly Democratic leadership will be keen to find ways to demonstrate that they still care about genuine concerns from the Jewish community, one would hope that these are pursued with a more concrete grounding in reality and shared security than as a tool for repressing pro-Palestinian speech.

But many in the Democratic base would like to see the party do much more – including holding hearings into the US role in enabling Israel’s genocide in Gaza, a topic that would ensnare senior officials from the Biden administration in a very public accounting that the establishment is keen to avoid.

Here is where the details of the outcome of the midterms will truly matter. While there is no doubt that the centre point of the Democratic Congressional caucus has shifted to the left for the upcoming 120th Congress, particularly in the House, the size of the majority matters.

As recent Republican Houses have demonstrated, a small majority is a challenge for the speaker, as it empowers a small group of members to exert significant leverage through the threat of withdrawal of their support for basic procedural steps that are typically decided on a partisan vote basis.

As a result of the midterms “blue tsunami”, however, the Democratic majority is secure enough that leadership will have to make few real concessions to the left of their party, likely teeing up some tense, and almost inevitably public, tussling in the coming two years, particularly when it comes to appropriations bills.

In short, the Democrats’ campaign for legislative power has been a success, but particularly in the face of an imperious White House that has shown little interest in even longstanding legal precedent in its deference to Congress, it remains incomplete.

At the same time, being the party locked out of power has enabled the Democrats up to this point to dodge some degree of the internal wrangling that is already long overdue on key issues, such as foreign policy on Israel.

A majority in Congress may not give them complete control – but it does mean they will now own the legislative branch’s decisions. Whether they demonstrate a meaningful and proactive shift – or let themselves be constrained by establishment conservatism – may define the viability of their path to further electoral success in 2028.

Either way, the American people will be watching what Democrats do and do not do – as will the Republicans who, as Trump enters his “lame duck” years, are likely to undergo an evolution of their own on these key issues.

This makes progress in the coming Congress all the more acute an issue for the Democrats. The challenge for them is simple: take credible leadership on driving change or face the very real possibility of being outflanked by the “America First” right.

articles.title: Fox News Voter Poll: 2026 midterm elections usher in a blue wave as Democrats win control of Congress
articles.summary: President Donald hTrump's job approval sank to 38% as inflation, tariffs and the Iran war drove a historic Democratic sweep of the House and the Senate.
articles.body: In a historic midterm election, Democrats swept both the House and Senate, riding a blue wave spurred by widespread voter discontent. The economy, government corruption, war in Iran and increasingly negative views of President Donald Trump's job performance created a perfect storm for Democrats to flip Senate seats in Republican stronghold states. At the time of publication, Democrats held a 54-seat majority in the Senate and have secured 228 seats in the House. The toss-up Senate race in Alaska remains too close to call at this time. The Fox News Voter Poll surveyed more than 100,000 registered voters nationwide from Oct. 19 to Nov. 3, 2026, combining online and telephone interviews with in-person surveys of Election Day voters. After the strong rightward shifts in the 2024 election, this year’s midterms marked a turn back to the left. The electorate remained divided by community type, gender and education, a pattern that has become commonplace in recent elections. Suburban and urban voters, women and Hispanics sided with Democrats, while rural voters, men and voters without a college degree favored Republicans. STATE OF PLAY: BLUE WAVE SWEEPS DEMOCRATS INTO POWER, WITH KEY RACES STILL HANGING IN BALANCE Groups that helped power Trump’s 2024 win — namely rural, Hispanic, young and independent voters — moved decidedly toward Democrats. DEMOCRAT SEIZE HOUSE CONTROL IN STUNNING BLUE TSUNAMI, VOW RETRIBUTION AGAINST TRUMP ADMIN A pivotal group in his win, rural voters backed Trump by 28 points in 2024. That advantage dropped by 10 points, to just 18 points in favor of Republican House candidates. Republicans underperformed among rural women. After Trump carried them by 21 points in 2024, Republican House candidates led among them by 8 points this year, a 13-point decline. At the same time, suburban women marched firmly toward Democrats. Harris won them by a 14-point margin, and they broke for Democratic House candidates by 24 points. That shift extended beyond community divides. Hispanic voters, who showed surprising support for Trump two years ago, backed Democratic House candidates by 27 points, after breaking for Harris by just 12 points. This was driven largely by Hispanic men, who after narrowly voting for Harris by 2 points in 2024, sided with the Democrats by 15 points. Young voters also followed a similar pattern. Often considered a reliable Democratic voting bloc, those under age 30 defied conventional wisdom and narrowly backed Harris by 4 points in 2024. Now, they backed Democratic House candidates by nearly 3-to-1. ‘LAWYER UP’: DEMS IMMEDIATELY PUT TRUMP ON NOTICE AMID REPUBLICANS' MIDTERM BLOODBATH Young men made a complete reversal in their party preference, going from a 15-point margin for Trump to a 33-point margin for the Democratic House candidates, a 48-point swing. Slightly more Democrats than Republicans backed their party’s House candidates. While there was a small amount of defections on the right, the bigger move came from the middle. Independents backed Democratic candidates by 22 points, a 16-point shift from 2024, when they backed Harris by just 6 points. Within the Republican Party, the divide between MAGA and non-MAGA Republicans widened. A narrow majority of Republicans (54%) considered themselves MAGA, and they voted almost unanimously for Republican candidates (99%). Fewer non-MAGA Republicans stayed with their party (85%). Beyond the demographic shifts, this was an election cycle marked by voter pessimism, economic frustration and disillusionment with the Republican brand. Voters cast their ballots with a bleak view of the country in their minds. Three-quarters said they felt dissatisfied or angry about how things were going, while just a quarter were satisfied or enthusiastic. The anger divides along partisan lines: more than 6 in 10 Democrats were angry with how things were going, compared with 1 in 10 Republicans and more than a third of independents. This is a reversal from the 2022 midterms, when roughly half of Republicans were angry, compared with 15% of Democrats and 27% of independents. Frustration with the present extended into the future. Half said they expected life for the next generation to be worse than life today, twice the share who expected it to be better. Voters took those frustrations out on the president. Trump’s job approval stood at 38%-62%, a net rating of -24, and that disapproval was intense. More than half strongly disapproved of his job performance, double the number who strongly approved. Eight years ago, at the midterm point in his first term, his job approval rating was a stronger 44%-56%, a net rating of just -12. Even without Trump on the ballot, he was on the minds of many Americans. More said they cast their House vote to express opposition to him than to support him, nearly a 3-to-1 margin. Part of that opposition came from a sense that Trump did not understand what voters were going through. More voters said Trump prioritized his own personal interests than the country’s. They also gave him low marks on personal traits. More than 6 in 10 said he lacked the right priorities and did not fight for people like them. Narrow majorities said he was not a strong leader and lacked the mental capability to serve effectively. The president’s standing was also a drag on his party. Two years after winning unified control of Washington, the Republican Party was -18 points underwater, a -15-point slide from its net rating of -3 in 2024. The Democratic Party was unpopular as well, but its net rating held nearly steady, from -7 to -6. Each party’s voters were about equally loyal: nearly all Republicans and Democrats viewed their own party favorably. Independents were more favorable toward the Democrats, with 42% viewing the Democratic Party favorably, while they rated the Republican Party negatively by about 2-to-1. Views of the party also tracked the views of its leader. Democrats were nearly unanimous in their disapproval of Trump, while about 8 in 10 Republicans approved. Roughly 7 in 10 independents viewed the president unfavorably. Two years ago, voters gave the Republicans a chance to bring prices down. This year, they said tariffs, inflation and a war in Iran pushed costs higher, and they used this election to call for change. The effects of inflation were inescapable for the majority, including 1 in 5 who called that hardship severe. Three-quarters rated the economy negatively, a stark reversal from this point in Trump’s first term, when positive ratings outnumbered negative ones by 2-to-1, as shown in the 2018 Fox News Voter Analysis survey (66% positive, 34% negative). Almost 7 in 10 of voters who gave the economy a negative rating voted for the Democrats. Among those with a positive economic outlook, Republicans were favored. Within the household budget, concerns about prices varied little across categories. The cost of gas and diesel was at the top, a worry that followed the Iran war and its effect on fuel prices. Healthcare and groceries were right behind, and a majority were very concerned about utilities. Voters’ views on Iran were closely linked to fuel costs. In general, about 6 in 10 believed the U.S. made the wrong decision in taking military action, and they backed the Democratic House candidate. Nearly all voters who called it the right decision supported Republicans. In an exclusive survey by Fox News and NORC at the University of Chicago, voters were asked about various priorities regarding the Iran war. The survey of approximately 3,000 registered voters was conducted Nov. 1–3 by phone and online using NORC’s probability-based AmeriSpeak panel. More than two-thirds said it was very important to avoid a prolonged conflict in Iran, while half said the same about stopping Iran from developing nuclear weapons. Ultimately, gas prices took priority over security threats. When asked to choose, nearly twice as many voters preferred ending military involvement to bring down gas prices as preferred restarting military action to stop nuclear weapons development. More than 8 in 10 Democrats favored ending the conflict to bring down gas prices, as did around 6 in 10 independents. The same share of Republicans, 6 in 10, favored restarting military action. Still, just over half of Republicans saw it as very important to avoid a prolonged conflict in the region, as did a majority of Democrats and independents. When it comes to higher-than-usual prices, voters were considerably more likely to point to Trump’s policies than to factors outside his control. A majority said his policies had made conditions in the U.S. worse, while fewer said they improved conditions. Tariffs were a central piece of that blame. About two-thirds said Trump’s tariffs hurt the national economy and nearly as many said they hurt the economy in their own area. About 2 in 10 said tariffs helped the national economy, and even fewer said they helped locally. While families wrestled with high prices, voters felt Trump was more focused on his own interests than the people he serves. That frustration extended to the economic system itself: nearly 7 in 10 said it favored the wealthy. Yet that skepticism coexisted with support for capitalism. More than half of voters viewed capitalism favorably, far more than the third who viewed socialism favorably. Voters liked the idea of the system but doubted how it worked for them. Government corruption and the cost of living were the two main drivers of the vote, with roughly half calling each crucial. Immigration and the Iran war followed closely, each crucial for more than a third, with AI and data centers further back. Democrats were the favored party among voters who said corruption, costs, Iran and AI were crucial to their vote, while Republicans held their edge with voters focused on immigration. Frustration with costs and corruption was reflected in how voters saw the state of the country. The economy topped the list of issues facing the country, narrowly ahead of the state of democracy. Immigration came in a distant third, followed by healthcare, foreign policy and crime. The prominence of democracy came mainly from Democrats, who named the state of democracy as their top issue (48%), ahead of the economy (36%). Independents put the economy first (39%), with democracy close behind (34%). Republicans ranked democracy third (16%), behind the economy (41%) and immigration (27%). Voters who named democracy and the economy as their top issue backed Democratic House candidates, while voters who prioritized immigration backed Republicans. Democrats also held an advantage when it came to which party would do a better job handling six of the eight issues tested, though often by modest margins. Their largest edge was on healthcare, followed by transgender policies. On the economy — the issue voters saw as the most important facing the country — Democrats led by 6 points, similar to their margins on foreign policy (+5). On government corruption, voters narrowly favored Democrats, but a third did not trust either party to handle one of the top issues facing the country. Republicans led only on immigration, with a 3-point lead. The parties ran even on taxes and finished within two points of each other on AI. On healthcare, concern about costs was widespread, and those voters backed the Democratic House candidates. A clear majority favored a bigger federal role in helping Americans get care. Consequently, they gave the Trump administration poor marks on the issue, with majorities saying its policies made it harder to get the care they needed and made their own costs worse. On AI, voters approached this new political issue with wariness. A majority said it would do more to hurt society, a consensus reached by Democrats, Republicans and independents alike, while a quarter said it would do more to help. Among partisans, Republicans were the most likely to say AI would have a positive impact on society, at 33%. At this point, neither party had a clear advantage on the issue: AI drew the highest share, choosing neither party as better able to handle it, and the two parties finished within 2 points of each other, with Democrats narrowly pulling ahead. Data center construction drew a similar verdict. Three-quarters of voters opposed a new data center in their community. Those who opposed one backed the Democratic House candidates by 28 points, while those in favor backed Republicans by 45 points. Among rural voters, data centers had emerged as a defining issue. They also split 3-to-1 in opposition to building one in their community. On immigration, Republicans were favored to handle, but voters delivered a verdict of overreach on enforcement. A majority said the Trump administration’s actions had gone too far, with the rest split between about right and not far enough. Immigration and Customs Enforcement received mostly negative marks, with a majority of voters disapproving of its job performance. Most voters viewed immigrants favorably, saying they do more to help the country than to hurt it. Ratings of the institutions themselves were low. Congress drew approval from roughly a quarter, and the Supreme Court drew approval from about 4 in 10. Voters wanted a stronger Congress. A majority said Congress was not doing enough to provide checks and balances on the presidency, and those voters backed Democratic House candidates by 49 points. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Fox News Voter Poll is a survey conducted by SSRS with more than 100,000 registered voters nationwide. This survey was conducted Oct. 19 to Nov. 3, 2026, concluding at the end of voting on Election Day. The poll combines data collected from registered voters online and by telephone with data collected in-person from Election Day voters at precincts across the country. In the final step, all the pre-election survey respondents and Election Day exit poll respondents are combined by adjusting the share of voting mode (absentee, early-in-person and Election Day) based on the estimated composition of the national electorate. Once votes are counted, the survey results are also weighted to match the national election results. Results among all registered voters interviewed nationwide have an estimated margin of sampling error of plus or minus 0.5 percentage points, including the design effects. The error margin is larger among subgroups. Full methodological details are available here. The Fox News/NORC AmeriSpeak Study is a national survey of registered voters conducted by NORC at the University of Chicago. This survey was conducted Nov. 1–3, 2026, concluding as polls close on Election Day. The poll is based on a random sample of approximately 3,000 registered voters drawn from NORC’s probability-based AmeriSpeak panel, interviewed online and by telephone in English and Spanish. Survey weights adjust to population totals for demographic and geographic characteristics, as well as voter-specific information including partisanship, and, once votes are counted, the results are weighted to the national popular vote for the House of Representatives. Results among all 3,464 registered voters interviewed nationwide have an estimated margin of sampling error of plus or minus 2.5 percentage points, including the design effects. The error margin is larger among subgroups.

articles.title: Democrats score key secretary of state wins ahead of the 2028 election
articles.summary: Democrats won secretary of state contests in four presidential battlegrounds while making inroads in red territory, giving them election oversight authority in key states for the 2028 elections.
articles.body: Democrats won secretary of state contests in four presidential battlegrounds while making inroads in red territory, giving them election oversight authority in key states for the 2028 elections. Democratic candidates maintained control of secretary of state offices in Arizona, Michigan and Nevada, while flipping the office in Georgia, all states that have been at the center of recent campaigns for the White House. And Democrats gained secretary of state control in the GOP-leaning states of Indiana and Ohio. Follow live coverage In Georgia, Democrat Penny Brown Reynolds will succeed Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger, who drew President Donald Trump’s ire for rebuffing his push to overturn the state’s 2020 election results. She defeated state Rep. Tim Fleming, a former aide to outgoing Republican Gov. Brian Kemp who was endorsed by Trump. Reynolds, who is known for a family court television show and serving in the Biden administration, campaigned as a judge who would stand up to Trump while following the law in running state elections. Fleming did not go as far as other Republicans in claiming the 2020 election was stolen, but said there were “irregularities” and called for new mail voting restrictions. In Michigan, Democratic Lt. Gov Garlin Gilchrist bested Macomb County Clerk Anthony Forlini, a Republican, to succeed Democratic Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, who won the state’s race for governor. Gilchrist had criticized Forlini for sharing voter data with the Trump administration and hiring a Jan. 6 protester to his office. In Arizona and Nevada, incumbent Democrats Adrian Fontes and Cisco Aguilar fended off challenges from far-right Republicans whose careers were rooted in advancing election conspiracy theories, enjoying far better margins than they had in similar 2022 matchups. And in Texas, Democrat Gina Hinojosa’s win in the governor’s race is also expected to give the party authority over the administration of state elections. Texas’ secretary of state is appointed by the governor, with concurrent terms. Once an under-the-radar, downballot job, secretary of state has become a much more high-profile position amid a constant drumbeat of unfounded election fraud claims from Trump and his allies. All four battleground states saw challenges to the 2020 election results and secretaries of state in these and other states have faced a steady stream of lawsuits and threats. In the final stretch of the midterm campaign, Democrats started targeting Indiana, Kansas, Ohio and Iowa for red-state gains. So far, they’ve won two of their targets and lost one. Democratic state Rep. Allison Russo will be the next secretary of state of Ohio as her party also flipped Senate and gubernatorial seats in a state that has shifted to the right in recent years. Russo defeated Republican state Treasurer Robert Sprague. In Indiana, Beau Bayh, a 30-year-old scion of a longtime Democratic family in the state, beat Republican state Rep. Max Engling. Engling had replaced Indiana’s Republican incumbent, Diego Morales, who was embroiled in allegations of corruption and ethics violations, at the party’s nominating convention. Bayh spent more than $ 8.6 million on ads, according to AdImpact, campaigning heavily on fighting corruption. He ran at the top of the ticket in Indiana, which didn’t have any races for Senate or governor this year. In Kansas, where voters haven’t elected a Democrat as secretary of state since 1948, the race between Democratic state Rep. Jennifer Day and Republican state Rep. Pat Proctor was too close to call, according to NBC News’ Decision Desk. Democrats saw success elsewhere in the state, with pastor Adam Hamilton pulling off an upset over GOP Sen. Roger Marshall. Top-of-the-ticket wins didn’t translate to secretary of state success everywhere. In Iowa, Republican Secretary of State Paul Pate fended off a challenge from Democrat Ryan Peterman, even as Democrats won Senate and governor’s races in the state. And In South Carolina, Republican Secretary of State Mark Hammond beat Democratic challenger Jason Belton, even as Democrat Annie Andrews prevailed in the Senate race.
