articles.title: JUSTIN HASKINS: 3 huge reasons Republicans lost. Here’s what they need to win in 2028
articles.summary: The 2026 midterm elections exposed three critical Republican failures, from the affordability crisis to the Iran war, that could reshape the 2028 race.
articles.body: The 2026 midterm elections are over, and Republicans have some serious questions to answer. Political strategists and pundits will undoubtedly spend weeks debating what went wrong, who deserves the blame and what the results mean for the 2028 presidential election. But the biggest lessons of this election should already be clear. Three major failures have left Republicans vulnerable, and unless conservatives address them soon, the political consequences could extend far beyond this election. 1. Conservatives need an exciting vision for the future. JASON CHAFFETZ: FIVE TIMELESS POLITICAL LESSONS THAT GOT LOST IN 2026 The first and perhaps most important problem is that Republicans have failed to offer Americans an exciting, ambitious vision for the future. Whatever you think about socialists and their radical proposals, there’s no denying that they have a grand vision for transforming society. They promise to fundamentally remake the economy, restructure major institutions and create an entirely different kind of America. THE NUMBERS DON’T LIE. YOUNG AMERICANS ARE FALLING IN LOVE … WITH SOCIALISM Where is the conservative alternative? Ask the average Republican politician what America would look like if conservatives achieved all their political goals and you’ll probably hear something about lowering taxes and securing the border. Those are certainly important objectives, but they hardly constitute the kind of sweeping, transformative vision that can inspire millions of Americans, especially younger voters. MORE AMERICANS THAN EVER NOW HAVE A POSITIVE VIEW OF SOCIALISM, NEW POLL SAYS Conservatives desperately need their own version of a political utopia, a radical vision of a better future that goes far beyond simply opposing whatever new proposal Democrats introduce. Imagine an America in which small businesses and families, rather than politically connected corporations, are the primary beneficiaries of tax and regulatory policy. Imagine a country where taxes are low and flat, where federal spending has been dramatically reduced, where innovation and entrepreneurship flourish, and where ordinary Americans have far greater control over their economic futures. AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI Perhaps most importantly, imagine a society in which the federal government has relinquished enormous amounts of power to state and local governments, allowing Americans with vastly different political and cultural values to live in communities that reflect their own priorities. Such a transformation would allow Americans to pursue dramatically different visions of the good life without constantly fighting over which ideology should control the federal government. DOUG SCHOEN: THE BIGGEST WINNER AND THE BIGGEST LOSER IN THE 2026 MIDTERMS This is the kind of ambitious, exciting vision that conservatism should be advancing. Unfortunately, far too many Republican politicians seem more interested in tinkering around the edges of an increasingly dysfunctional federal government than fundamentally transforming it. 2. The affordability crisis has not been solved. The second major problem is that Republicans failed to solve the affordability crisis that helped propel President Donald Trump back into the White House in 2024. Conservatives desperately need their own version of a political utopia, a radical vision of a better future that goes far beyond simply opposing whatever new proposal Democrats introduce. For millions of Americans, the most important political issue has been the rising cost of housing, food, energy and other necessities. Prices skyrocketed during the Biden administration, leaving families struggling to maintain their standard of living. BILLIONS SPENT BY KEY FEDERAL AGENCY HASN'T MADE AMERICAN DREAM OF HOMEOWNERSHIP ANY EASIER: REPORT Trump and Republicans promised to fix these problems, and although they have made some progress, the affordability crisis remains largely unresolved. Consider housing. According to the Federal Housing Finance Agency’s seasonally adjusted Purchase-Only House Price Index, home prices increased 54% between January 2020 and December 2024. From January 2025 through August 2026, the most recent month for which data are available, home prices increased another 2.8%. That’s a significant improvement over the previous administration, but it’s a far cry from returning prices to their pre-pandemic levels. And home prices are only part of the affordability equation. Mortgage interest rates remain high, dramatically increasing the cost of financing a home purchase. The combination of historically elevated home prices and expensive mortgages has made homeownership increasingly difficult for millions of Americans, especially younger families trying to purchase their first home. The same basic problem exists throughout much of the economy. The rate of inflation might be lower than it was during the Biden administration, but that does little to help families who are still paying dramatically more for everyday necessities than they were just a few years ago. To their credit, Trump and congressional Republicans have implemented important reforms that should help improve the economy over time, including substantial deregulation, pro-energy policies and legislation making major provisions of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act permanent. Unfortunately, they have also wasted valuable time pursuing or considering big-government policies, including additional corporate subsidies and federal ownership stakes in private companies. Even more troubling, Republicans have continued running enormous federal budget deficits. Excessive deficit-financed government spending can contribute to inflation by increasing demand without producing a corresponding increase in the supply of goods and services. When demand grows faster than supply, prices tend to rise. With the help of billionaire Elon Musk, the Trump administration attempted to impose steep spending cuts through its new Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE). But Democrats and countless media outlets successfully and dishonestly undermined that effort, and congressional Republicans took the bait. Rather than cut spending, Republicans continued to add to America’s ballooning national debt. In fiscal year 2026, the deficit hit $1.99 trillion, and it will likely be even worse next year. The solution requires a much more aggressive approach: dramatically reducing federal spending, pursuing policies that sustainably lower borrowing costs and interest rates, and eliminating regulatory barriers that prevent businesses from expanding the supply of important goods and services, especially housing and energy. 3. The war remains unpopular. The third major problem is the Trump administration’s handling of the war in Iran. Regardless of whether you support the war, there’s little question that Trump failed to convince large numbers of Americans that the conflict should be among the nation’s highest priorities. That failure was particularly damaging because the war created significant divisions within Trump’s own political coalition. For millions of Americans, the most important political issue has been the rising cost of housing, food, energy and other necessities. Prices skyrocketed during the Biden administration, leaving families struggling to maintain their standard of living. Some conservatives strongly supported military action against Iran, believing it was necessary to protect American interests and prevent future threats. Others questioned whether another prolonged Middle Eastern conflict was consistent with the priorities Trump campaigned on. These disagreements were always going to create political challenges. But during an election year, when Republicans desperately needed a unified political coalition, they were especially costly. The situation was made even worse by the economic consequences of the conflict. Higher gasoline and energy prices placed additional pressure on Americans already struggling with the affordability crisis. Meanwhile, the fighting continued far longer than the administration initially suggested it would. For voters who supported Trump because they wanted Washington to focus on the problems facing Americans at home, the prolonged conflict undoubtedly raised difficult questions about the administration’s priorities. None of this necessarily means the war was unjustified or that military action was the wrong decision. There are serious arguments on both sides of that debate. But when a president commits the country to a major military conflict, especially one with significant economic consequences, he must convince Americans that the sacrifices are necessary and that the objectives are worth pursuing. Ultimately, the lessons of the 2026 midterms extend far beyond the question of which political party controls Congress. America is approaching another consequential presidential election, and the ideological battles that will shape the country’s future are only becoming more important. articles.title: Ballot measure takeaways: Voters back abortion rights, along with photo ID and citizenship requirements at the polls
articles.summary: In ballot measures across the country Tuesday, voters mostly expressed support for abortion rights, while affirming voter identification requirements and upholding that only U.S. citizens can vote in state elections.
articles.body: In ballot measures across the country Tuesday, voters mostly expressed support for abortion rights, while affirming voter identification requirements and upholding that only U.S. citizens can vote in state elections. Nearly 150 ballot measures were at stake in more than three dozen states. The most prominent, and expensive, initiative was a proposed billionaire tax in California, but the outcome remained uncertain as votes continued to be tallied Wednesday. Still, voters directly determined the direction of policies in their states related to other taxes, voting issues, transgender rights and more. Here is a roundup of the most notable ballot measure results. Abortion rights Four ballot measures asked voters to amend their state constitutions in ways that would affirm or retract abortion rights. In Nevada and Virginia, where abortion access through fetal viability is legal, voters weighed in on ballot measures that would enshrine those rights in each state’s constitution. Voters in both states overwhelmingly passed those initiatives by a margin of at least 24 percentage points. In Nevada, the vote was the second on the measure because the state constitution requires citizen-initiated constitutional amendments to pass in two consecutive general elections. In Missouri, voters rejected a GOP-backed ballot measure that proposed stripping language enshrining abortion rights from the state constitution that had been added in 2024. That year, voters approved a constitutional amendment to protect abortion rights until fetal viability. However, in ruby-red Idaho — where abortion is almost completely banned — voters roundly rejected a ballot measure that would have created a statutory right to an abortion through fetal viability. Wealth taxes In Washington state, voters rejected a ballot measure that would have repealed the state’s so-called millionaires tax — a 9.9% tax on annual income over $1 million that Democratic lawmakers enacted just earlier this year. Meanwhile, California’s billionaire tax, on the ballot as Proposition 40, was trailing by 11 points with 60% of the expected vote in. Voter ID and citizenship requirements Voters in nearly a dozen states also decided on ballot measures that mostly reiterated existing laws regarding voter identification requirements and barring noncitizens from casting ballots in state elections. West Virginia, South Dakota, Kansas, Alaska and Arkansas voters all approved constitutional amendments affirming that only U.S. citizens can vote in state elections. The laws are expected to prevent any local jurisdictions from moving to allow noncitizens to vote in local elections, which some municipalities have sought to do in recent years. The initiatives appeared on the ballot amid the Trump administration’s broader crackdown on noncitizen voting, which is extremely rare. Voters in Ohio, North Carolina and Nevada passed measures to add to their state constitutions the requirements that residents present photo ID when voting in person. In Virginia, voters approved a Democratic-backed measure to enshrine in their state constitution the restoration of all felons’ right to vote after their release from prison. In Massachusetts, voters rejected a measure that would have replaced party primary elections with a top-two all-party primary. Redistricting The mid-decade redistricting war also extended to the ballot, with voters in two states siding with Democrats. In Missouri, voters blocked a GOP-drawn congressional map from going into effect after a long-running legal battle. The new lines sought to carve up one of the state’s two Democratic-held districts. Maryland voters, meanwhile, approved a constitutional amendment paving the way for Democrats to redraw their state’s congressional map. The state has just one district represented by a Republican. Transgender rights Republicans and conservative groups also placed a series of measures targeting transgender individuals on the ballot in several states, including Arizona, Colorado and Washington. Several were still too early to call as of Wednesday, but in Arizona, voters approved a GOP-backed measure requiring schools to designate sports and intramural teams as male, female or coed based on athletes’ sex assigned at birth.

articles.title: Fox News/NORC Study: Voters look to 2028 focused on the economy
articles.summary: As the 2028 race for the White House looms, grocery prices, gas costs and healthcare top what voters want newly elected officials to tackle first.
articles.body: After the midterm elections, attention will turn to the 2028 race for the White House. What is on voters’ minds as they look ahead to the next presidential election? Most Republicans want the next president to follow President Donald Trump’s policies, if not his style. Nearly 4 in 10 MAGA Republicans want Trump’s successor to emulate both, and about half want the next president to follow his policies alone. Non-MAGA Republicans are less enthusiastic: 45% want his policies to continue, but only about 15% of non-MAGA Republicans want a president with the same style. Independents prefer something entirely different: 6 in 10 want the next president to break with both Trump’s policies and his style. Likewise, few Democrats want to see either his style or his policies repeated. Even as the Democrats have won control of the Senate and the House of Representatives, and Trump finds his approval rating at 39%, a bloc of voters remains loyal to the president and is likely to influence the 2028 campaign. While half of voters want a successor who does not emulate his style or follow his policies, 26% want a president who will carry on his policies, and another 12% want the next president to copy his policies and his style. FOX NEWS VOTER POLL: 2026 MIDTERM ELECTIONS USHER IN A BLUE WAVE AS DEMOCRATS WIN CONTROL OF CONGRESS Looking ahead, voters across party lines say improving economic conditions is the most important issue for the country to address over the next five years. Six in 10 voters feel they are holding steady financially while about 3 in 10 feel they are falling behind. Few, about 1 in 10 voters, feel they are getting ahead financially. Voters who describe their own financial situation as less than satisfactory, or say they are falling behind, are more likely to name the economy as the top issue. What should Tuesday's winners prioritize once sworn into office? When asked what is most important for newly elected officials to work on first in 2027, 3 in 10 voters want elected officials to address grocery costs. About 2 in 10 want action on gas prices, and a similar share say they should work on healthcare and prescription drug costs. Slightly fewer are concerned about housing costs, while about 1 in 10 want officials to address electricity and other utility costs. Voters are closely divided on whether the country can look forward to better days or if the good days are behind us. And it’s linked to how they’re feeling financially. About two-thirds of those who say they are getting ahead financially are optimistic about the future. However, about two-thirds of voters who are falling behind financially think the country’s best days are in the past. Beyond the economy, priorities diverge. About 1 in 5 Democrats point to access to affordable healthcare, while about a similar share of Republicans say protecting individuals from government overreach is the top issue. About 1 in 10 independents say the country should address the affordability of healthcare, and about the same share say government overreach. Voters are divided over AI’s effect on the U.S. economy during the next 10 years. About 4 in 10 say it will be harmful, while 3 in 10 expect benefits. About 1 in 10 expect AI to make no difference, while slightly more, about 2 in 10, are unsure. About 4 in 10 expect AI to negatively affect the environment and the arts and entertainment industry. About half of voters want substantial changes in how the country is run. Party identification shapes how much change voters want and which branches of government they think most need reform. Democrats are about three times as likely as Republicans to want complete upheaval of how the country is run. Half of democratic socialists favor complete and total upheaval, compared with about 1 in 10 MAGA Republicans. In the 2024 Fox News Voter Analysis conducted for the presidential election, most Republican voters said they wanted substantial change or total upheaval. Now, with a Republican in the White House and their party controlling both houses of Congress, they are less eager for major change. FOX NEWS VOTER POLL: HOW DEMOCRATS TOOK CONTROL OF THE SENATE Overall, 4 in 10 voters think Congress should be substantially reformed, including three-quarters of MAGA Republicans and half of non-MAGA Republicans. Democrats are less likely to say Congress needs reform, but half say the executive branch should be improved. Few voters in either party want changes to the Constitution. Democrats are more likely than Republicans or independents to say the Supreme Court needs reform. Voters across party lines support term limits for Congress and Supreme Court justices. Democrats favor abolishing the Electoral College, but Republicans and independents are less enthusiastic. Most Republicans support limiting mail voting to people physically unable to vote in person. MAGA Republicans are more supportive of limiting mail voting than non-MAGA Republicans (63% vs 40%). Democrats oppose the idea, regardless of whether they support the Democratic Socialists of America. AMERICANS CLASH OVER SUPREME COURT EXPANSION AS FIGHT OVER 9 JUSTICES HEATS UP: ‘LET’S PACK IT NOW’ The expansion of artificial intelligence has triggered some public backlash against AI data centers. Voters are divided on whether AI will help or hurt during the next 10 years. More Democrats say the technology will be harmful while more Republicans expect benefits. Among Republican voters, MAGA Republicans are more enthusiastic about AI than non-MAGA Republicans. Forty-five percent of MAGA Republicans believe AI will help the U.S. to compete with other countries, and another 4 in 10 feel AI will do more to help the economy. Among Democrat voters, supporters of democratic socialism and those who do not support the movement are similarly likely to feel AI will help aspects of American society. However, supporters of democratic socialism are more likely than other Democrats to feel AI will do more to hurt than help. Overall, 6 in 10 voters are extremely or very concerned about the effect of data centers on the price of utilities in the communities where they are being built. About half are concerned about the effect of data centers on pollution of natural resources, land development or the health of the local population, regardless of whether they live near a data center. Democrats are more concerned about the effects of data centers than Republican voters, again, regardless of their proximity to the facilities. Voters across party lines support requiring companies to pay for electric grid upgrades needed for their data centers, increasing government regulation of AI, and limiting AI in schools. Most Democrats and independents oppose building a data center in their community. Most voters also oppose local construction, whether their county already has a data center. AMERICA’S MULTI-BILLION TECH BOOM COMES INTO FOCUS AS 7 KEY STATES PUT IT TO A MIDTERM TEST The economy is a top issue for most voters, yet 4 in 10 say they could support a candidate whose economic views differ from their own. After the economy and jobs, nearly 6 in 10 voters see healthcare as an important issue, and about 6 in 10 would not support a candidate who disagrees with them on healthcare policy. About half could not back a candidate whose views on Israel and the Palestinians differ from theirs. Overall, about 6 in 10 say they could never support a candidate they disagree with on abortion, guns, or immigration. Interviews were conducted in English and Spanish. articles.title: Vance courting disgruntled Trump voters to form ‘new right’ alliance after Republican bloodbath, sources say
articles.summary: JD Vance blamed the Iran war for the GOP's midterm losses and laid out four tasks he says will bring disaffected Republican voters back to the party.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: Vice President JD Vance is seeking to forge a new alliance with disaffected Trump voters ahead of the 2028 election cycle, Fox News Digital has learned. Vance took control of his own messaging Wednesday morning in the wake of a brutal Republican midterm beatdown, breaking with President Donald Trump on foreign policy and America's relationship with Israel. A source familiar with post-election happenings told Fox News Digital that there was a White House meeting Wednesday morning aimed at aligning the entire administration officials on post-midterm messaging. A second source familiar described the meeting as a regular senior staff meeting. After the meeting, Vance posted on X a lengthy assessment of the outcome, blaming the Iran war, just as President Donald Trump had done on Tuesday night when he called into Fox News during election coverag. VANCE'S SCATHING IRAN WAR POSTMORTEM PUTS POTENTIAL 2028 GOP SHOWDOWN IN FOCUS: 'EVERYONE KNOWS WHY' "The reason we lost is the war," Vance's post said. "The president himself said so last night." "If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest," he went on. "But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there." In the post, Vance said a pollster and "one of the smartest people I know in politics" laid out four tasks that would bring voters back to the GOP — end the war in Iran, focus on the cost of living and inflation, put America first, and "change our relationship with Israel." JD VANCE DECLINES TO ENDORSE NETANYAHU DESPITE TRUMP'S STRONG BACKING A Trump administration official who spoke with Fox News Digital said that the four tasks are Vance's rallying cry to the "new right," broadly defined as a coalition of Republicans that aligns with the president's original "America First" movement — staying out of foreign conflicts, making America an affordable place for Americans to raise families, and closing the borders. But those voters, they said, also believe that Trump is too aligned with Israel on foreign policy matters. Among some on the political right, the war in Iran is intrinsically tied to Israel's influence in the Middle East, and Trump's relationship with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. TRUMP TOLD DONORS 'WE NEED TO ELECT JD,' SOURCE CONFIRMS, AS HE WEIGHS VANCE OR RUBIO IN 2028 The official made it clear that Vance’s message is not a separation from Trump, à la former Vice President Mike Pence who denounced Trump after the Jan. 6, 2021, riot at the capitol. Rather, they said, he is aiming to send a clear message to Republicans who support Trump and disagree with or feel betrayed by his foreign policy. And that message is: "Vance is our guy." The White House did not return Fox News Digital's request for comment at time of publication on the meeting or Vance's post-election messaging. The vice president has not strayed much from Trump and the White House's preferred messaging for the past two years — though he has been one of the few voicing concern over the ongoing war in Iran. Despite his friendship with Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, reports and comments from the vice president himself have expressed how his stance on the Iran conflict differs. Trump acknowledged earlier this year that Vance was "maybe less enthusiastic" about attacking Iran from the jump. TRUMP 'COULDN'T TRANSFER THE LOVE' OF HIS SUPPORTERS TO OTHER REPUBLICANS AMID HISTORIC MIDTERM LOSS Vance is widely considered a top GOP presidential candidate in 2028 — along with Trump's Secretary of State Marco Rubio. So far, Democrats stand at 54 Senate seats to Republicans' 44, after sweeping wins in typically red Texas, ruby-red Kansas and other Republican strongholds like South Carolina. DEMS SEIZE THE SENATE AS BLUE TIDAL WAVE CRASHES DEEP INTO TRUMP COUNTRY, TOPPLES GOP STRONGHOLDS Votes are still being counted into Wednesday in a tight race in Alaska, that could see Democrats winning yet another seat in the Senate and widening their majority over the GOP. The outcome of the midterms could have massive implications for the 2028 election, and Republicans are grappling now with how to face one of their biggest-ever challenges in trying to flip back the upper chamber despite a widened gap throwing them deep into a minority in January. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Needing only 218 to control the House, Democrats on Wednesday afternoon had won 237 seats, with more projected to filter in as ballots are counted and races are called.

articles.title: 5 things to know after election night: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: Welcome to a special post-election edition of the From the Politics Desk newsletter!
articles.body: Welcome to a special post-election edition of the From the Politics Desk newsletter! Dive in below for the latest storylines around the House, Senate and state-level results. — Adam Wollner 5 things to know after election night The dust is continuing to settle following a momentous midterm election, with Democrats securing stunning victories up and down the ballot after voters delivered a stark rebuke to President Donald Trump and his party. Here is the latest on where things stand. Redistricting fell flat: Republicans redrew more than a dozen congressional districts in states such as Texas, Florida, Ohio and North Carolina ahead of the midterms in an aggressive attempt to shore up their narrow majority in Washington. However, Democrats may actually come out ahead in the 2026 redistricting war, or fight it to a draw, in part with massive upsets in some of these same states after overpowering the GOP maps, Ben Kamisar reports. Democrats will hold at least 11 of the 15 seats redrawn by Republicans before the election to benefit their party, with more gains possible depending on how the final votes fall. But that’s not all: They also picked up a seat in a Utah district that was redrawn by a court to their benefit, and they are poised to net as many as five seats in California, where Democrats did a redraw of their own. Republicans, meanwhile, lost Texas’ 15th District after making it more vulnerable as part of an ill-fated attempt to topple Democratic incumbents in South Texas. And they’re at risk of losing up to two more seats Republican lawmakers similarly watered down in other states. Democrats have so far gained a net of flipped 34 seats, giving them 242 seats to Republicans’ 150, with 43 races uncalled. A reordering in the House: Democrats are on the cusp of elevating Hakeem Jeffries to become the first Black speaker of the House. Meanwhile, Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., told his staff this morning he will not stay on as Republican leader in the new Congress. Democrats will face a tricky challenge when they take control of both chambers of Congress in January: carrying out aggressive an oversight of Trump and his administration while needing his signature to advance just about any legislative goal, Scott Wong and Sahil Kapur write. Democrats could still expand their Senate majority: As things currently stand, Democrats flipped seven Senate seats, bringing their total to 54 compared to 44 for the Republicans. Two Senate races remain uncalled: Alaska and Mississippi. In Alaska, Democrat Mary Pelotola has 48.2% support, while Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan has 47.9% with three-fourths of the expected vote in. But if no candidate eclipses a majority, the race will go to a ranked choice tabulation. And that could take weeks to resolve, as mail ballots that were postmarked by Election Day can be counted up to 15 days later. And in Mississippi, GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democrat Scot Colom are separated by less than 65 votes, with more than 95% of the vote tallied. According to Bridget Bowman, there is no mechanism for an election to undergo a recount under Mississippi state law, and both parties are signaling that they’re gearing up for a legal battle. Democratic gains extended to state level: In addition to flipping the House and the Senate, Democrats clinched a majority of governorships for the first time in 16 years, Adam Edelman notes. In five states, Democrats also secured a trifecta — winning control of the governorship and both chambers of the legislature — giving the party a level of power it hasn’t held in some of those places in years. And Democrats swept the secretary of state races that were on the ballot in key presidential battlegrounds, per Jane C. Timm, while flipping the office in two red-leaning states. GOP blame game: It didn’t take long for the finger-pointing among Republicans to begin after polls closed last night. Some wondered whether the party would finally break from Trump, who told voters to “pretend” he was on the ballot in the midterms, Matt Dixon, Garrett Haake and Allan Smith report. Vice President JD Vance said on X that the “real reason” for the GOP’s widespread losses was anger over Iran war. Meanwhile, in his first post-election public appearance, Trump boasted about the White House ballroom under construction and largely skirted talk about his party’s performance, Rebecca Shabad writes. That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.

articles.title: Republicans trade blame for historic midterm loss
articles.summary: Vice President JD Vance said the Iran war was the “real reason” for Tuesday’s losses.
articles.body:
The Republicans' devastating midterm losses prompted heated recriminations, as well as unofficial campaigning for the 2028 GOP presidential nomination.

President Donald Trump insisted he "wasn't on the ticket," after weeks of urging voters to "pretend I'm on the ballot." A defiant White House was quick to pin blame on the losing candidates , who in turn pointed fingers at the president's tariff policies and his unpopular war with Iran: Trump was " the engineer of the Republican collapse ," a GOP strategist told The New York Times.

Prominent Republicans like Florida's governor called for a reckoning , and early presidential frontrunner Vice President JD Vance earned plaudits for declaring that the Iran war was the " real reason " for Tuesday's losses.
